summary:
Sections 153 to 155 of the Penal Code criminalise sex between men. Anal intercourse carries up to fourteen years' imprisonment; attempts and assault with intent to commit it carry up to seven years; acts of gross indecency between males carry up to five years. Sex between women is not a criminal offence.

The provisions are not enforced in practice. A 2015 US State Department human rights report recorded no prosecutions under them, and no prosecution of an LGBTQ person under these sections has been reported.

There is no statutory protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Article 15(3) of the Constitution prohibits discrimination by reference to race, place of origin, political opinions, colour and creed, and does not address sexual orientation or gender identity. As of the 2015 reporting cycle, no non-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity was in force.

The Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015 is reported to prohibit employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation under Article 107(2)(b). The 2015 US State Department report described the position differently, finding gender-based discrimination prohibited only in the field of employment and poorly enforced in practice.

The Marriage Act (Cap 54) does not expressly bar recognition of same-sex marriages; its drafting assumes the parties are of opposite sex, and its restrictions on marriage cover relatives, parties below the age of 16, and bigamy. No mechanism for legal recognition of a same-sex partnership is sourced.

At the 21st session of the Universal Periodic Review, in 2016, France, Slovenia and Chile each urged Kiribati to decriminalise homosexuality. The Kiribati delegation made no response to those recommendations, but stated that it was considering advice, from Uruguay, to adopt legislation prohibiting discrimination covering gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation.

Kiribati voted at the UN General Assembly in November 2016 in favour of retaining the mandate of the Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the amendment to defund the mandate was rejected 84 to 77. Reporting on that vote identified Kiribati and Sri Lanka as the only two states that criminalised homosexuality yet supported the mandate's continuation, and also cited Kiribati, alongside Sri Lanka, among the states that still maintained anti-homosexuality laws at that date. No more recent status of the criminal provisions is sourced.
tangentialFactors:
Anthropological literature on the Pacific documents gender roles that do not map onto Western homosexual and transgender categories, including the Pinapinaaine or Binabinaaine role recorded for Kiribati and Tuvalu. A visitor should not assume that the absence of Western legal categories reflects the absence of local gender diversity, nor that local tolerance of such roles insulates a person from the Penal Code, which is drafted in terms of male conduct.

Kiribati's criminal provisions resemble those retained across parts of Oceania, but the source inventory supplies no comparative data on enforcement or penalties elsewhere in the region, so no regional ranking is offered here.

The 2015 US State Department reporting cycle recorded no societal discrimination or violence against LGBTQ people, alongside the finding that gender-based employment discrimination is poorly enforced. That finding rests on one reporting year and should be treated as a single data point rather than a general safety assessment for visitors, who are less likely than residents to appear in such reporting at all.
localsOnly:
Land ownership is restricted to I-Kiribati. This is a nationality-based restriction applying to residents and citizens generally, not a measure directed at LGBTQ people.

Gender-based discrimination is prohibited in law only in the field of employment, and the prohibition is described as poorly enforced. Residents have no general statutory remedy for discrimination on grounds of gender or, on the evidence sourced, sexual orientation outside employment.

Residents face the Penal Code sections directly, since the provisions apply to conduct within the territory regardless of the person's status; the reported absence of prosecutions is a matter of enforcement practice, not of legal immunity.

The Kiribati government's stated position at the 2016 Universal Periodic Review was that anti-discrimination legislation covering gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation was under consideration. Whether it was enacted is not sourced.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources disagree on the scope of employment protection. A secondary reference attributes a sexual-orientation employment discrimination ban to Article 107(2)(b) of the Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015, while the 2015 US State Department report describes only gender-based employment discrimination and calls it poorly enforced. No primary text of the Code is in the inventory; this conflict is unresolved here.

No source addresses entry or visa screening, including whether passport or travel-document gender markers are checked, amended, or a cause of secondary screening. Nothing is sourced on legal gender recognition, on access to gender-affirming medical care, or on prison placement for a trans detainee.

No reporting covers violence against trans people specifically. The only violence-adjacent finding is a general note that lesbians may face violence and discrimination, without incident dates, perpetrators or outcomes.

The most recent dated evidence in the inventory is the November 2016 UN General Assembly vote and the 2016 Universal Periodic Review cycle. Whether sections 153 to 155 remain in force and unamended after that date is not sourced.
